story|title:ai r d relevant model capabi.content_excerpt: This post presents evidence from our capability evaluations of public models relevant to AI R&D acceleration, up to Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. We remain significantly uncertain about central questions, including (1) what capabilities are in practice necessary for drastic acceleration, and (2) how quickly relevant model capabilities are improving. We think that current public evidence is insufficient to rule out drastic AI R&D acceleration in the next couple of years. By drastic AI R&D acceleration we mean a situation where capabilities improve so quickly that humans are no longer able to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems. This overview summarizes our main takeaways and their relevant sections within the post. 1 Background describes our motivation and aims, and how our thinking about capability evaluations has changed since the release of the original time horizons paper . 2 Methodology describes the different task sets used throughout the post, changes to human baselining methodology, and introduces our use of multiple score thresholds per task. 4 Robustness details various checks we did on our results, such as checking for reward hacking and refusals. We also investigate the effectiveness of agent swarms as an elicitation technique and find that they seem helpful on verifiable tasks with a clear metric and fast feedback (compared to best-of-k⁠ 5 ), and have unclear or negative effects on our other tasks. The appendices give more detail on our methodology, report robustness checks for our analyses, and highlight individual tasks with notable model behavior. In this post we focus on the measurement of capabilities relevant to accelerating AI R&D. A particularly salient uncertainty for AI R&D relevant capability evaluation is whether strong performance on ‘well-specified’ tasks alone is sufficient for drastic AI R&D acceleration, or whether other capabilities are needed. We aim to present evidence that is informative regardless of the reader’s view on this question. Historically, METR used our ‘time horizon’ metric as a way to measure the SWE-related agentic capabilities of AI systems.⁠ 6 Time horizon measurements were useful for risk assessments because (1) We considered the capabilities we were measuring with our time horizon suite to be necessary to pose catastrophic risk, (2) Our time horizon measurements were substantially grounded in human reference data, which made it easier to relate to risk relev

story|title:aletheia aegis deterministic.content_excerpt: Sub-millisecond runtime enforcement and output safety for autonomous AI agents. Fail-closed on credentials & life-safety. A deterministic, sub-millisecond guard for model outputs. Fail-closed on irreversible harm, fast enough to sit on every response, with an optional semantic judge for the cases patterns cannot settle. Aegis is the output plane of the Aletheia safety framework. It inspects generated text before it reaches a user, blocks credential leaks and life-safety failures outright, and flags everything else for audit or disclaimer. It runs offline by default, on CPU, with no response text retained. Built for platform, security, and AI infrastructure teams deploying tool-using agents into regulated or high-throughput production environments. Production agents need safety that does not break the product. The common approach, running a second LLM as judge on 100 percent of outbound traffic, fails on three counts at scale: Aegis takes the opposite starting point: enforce the non-negotiable invariants deterministically, at wire speed, and reserve model judgment for the small set of cases where semantics actually matter. That is the core design bet. Deterministic first, semantic second, fail-closed throughout. Stage 1: Deterministic edge engine. Every output is evaluated on CPU in 0.019 to 0.029 ms at p95. Irreversible failures trigger an immediate hard block. The upstream judge is skipped entirely, which saves cost and removes the exfiltration path. Stage 2: Optional semantic judge. For subjective or complex epistemic checks, an external judge (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini) can be called under strict rubrics. Detected secrets are masked before dispatch, life-safety findings can never be overruled, and heuristic defenses catch reviewer-targeted prompt injections. Aletheia standardizes nine failure signatures across the agentic lifecycle, grounded in 2,571 real-world incident records from the AI Incident Database, AVID, and the MIT AI Risk Repository. Aegis covers the output plane. Its companion, aletheia-mcp, covers the action plane. S3 is split by plane by design, so no single layer is a single point of failure: Benchmarked on Linux x86_64 and Apple Silicon, Node.js 18/20/22, single core unless noted. Held-out evaluation used 575 real model outputs across 30+ open and frontier models. Batches 10-11 replay offline with no external API cost: Labels were committed before measurement. The 90.2 percent figure is the balanced-policy result with the semantic judge

story|title:antseed brings people s comp.content_excerpt: Run the gateway and route every agent’s requests across the network on your rules. Your keys, your budgets, no middleman. Antseed runs on your computer. Your chat, your agents and your apps all go through it. A provider sees a peer ID, not your name. By default it can read your prompt. With a verified trusted execution environment (TEE), even the server operator can’t read it. A direct connection removes the intermediary. The provider can still read what it serves unless you choose a verified TEE. Models remember obscure facts differently, including their mistakes. Auditors ask fresh questions and compare the error rate with a trusted reference. Domain and GitHub verifications establish the provider’s identity. ANTS staking backs its reputation. Your device uses these signals to help choose who serves your requests. Serve open models on your GPUs, capacity you hold, a router you built, a specialized service or an agent. Set your terms, build your reputation and reach buyers across the network. Join together with others and let your machine serve while you’re away. We started the first one, Antseed Colony. The idea is a network of many Colonies. A fully peer-to-peer network for AI — like BitTorrent for inference. Buyers connect directly to independent providers, with no middleman. Anyone can supply intelligence, on their own terms. Use the gateway to manage shared access: run your own endpoint on a server and give each agent, app, or teammate their own API key, with budgets and the models and providers you choose. Use Antseed Desktop to connect the tools on your computer, without deploying a server. Both reach the same network. OpenRouter is a centralized aggregator: it decides which models are listed, routes every request through its own servers, and holds provider payouts until withdrawal. Antseed removes the aggregator from routing. Requests go peer-to-peer, payments settle onchain directly to the provider's wallet, and anyone can provide, no approval needed. story|title:clawdos an ai coding agent f.content_excerpt: An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier. Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware? I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box. As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle. Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off. The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS. Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API. story|title:find and serve fast llm conf.content_excerpt: Measures which LLM serving settings pay off on your GPU and your traffic, then serves the winner. Benchmarks vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp configurations; one OpenAI-compatible AP I got tired of guessing serving flags. Every guide says something different, and what's fastest on one GPU is often slower on another. So I built a tool that just measures. rigtune tries engines, weight precisions, KV-cache types and speculative decoding on your card, with your prompts, and then serves whatever won behind an OpenAI-compatible API. In November 2026 I tested it against everything I could find: stock vLLM and SGLang, vLLM's own auto_tune , BentoML's llm-optimizer, and the settings each engine's docs recommend. On Qwen3.5-9B it ran at least 1.8× faster than all of them. On Gemma 4 12B it found a completely different trick and beat the best expert setting by 1.5–1.7×. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, a mixture-of-experts model, on an H200, it ran 2.26× faster than stock vLLM. The answers held up every time, graded on GSM8K. ‡ The H200 run was vLLM only, against stock, bare stock, stock with fp8 weights (1,233 tok/s) and vLLM's expert rows. Its answers were graded on 300 GSM8K items, the others on all 1,319. What won. On Qwen it was the model's own multi-token-prediction (MTP) head, which sits in the checkpoint and is off by default. On the H200 it added fp8 weights and an fp8 KV cache, which the Ampere runs left out. On Gemma it was suffix decoding, which reuses text from the prompt. Different model and card, different winner. That's the whole reason to measure instead of guess. How it was measured. vLLM 0.33.0 and SGLang 0.5.23. rigtune tuned on 300 Dolly prompts, then every row was measured three times, interleaved, on 300 prompts it never saw. Every other tool got the same card, the same hour and the same latency limits. I tried AIConfigurator too, but it had no data for the A40 or for Qwen3.5's hybrid layers, so it couldn't give an answer. The H200 run is one command on Modal , about $10, if you want to check it yourself ( how ). Why the answer check matters. On my first run every row scored about 18% on GSM8K, stock included. Qwen3.5 thinks by default, and every answer ran out of tokens mid-thought. I nearly read that as "the speedup breaks accuracy". rigtune now turns thinking off for grading when the chat template has a switch for it. The A100 answers were graded by the comparison itself. story|title:how public evals work and fa.content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. story|title:leaky ai supply chain is exp.content_excerpt: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. story|title:npm package installed hermes.content_excerpt: The malicious npm package @leadstack/crm-connect installed a full AI agent on the servers it reached. It posed as the official client for a CRM called LeadStack. On install it set up Hermes Agent, an open-source agent from Nous Research that can run shell commands, edit files and drive a browser. It downloaded the agent’s keys and standing instructions from the attacker’s server and connected the agent to the attacker’s Telegram bot. Then it registered the agent as a systemd service renamed “LeadStack Lead Routing Daemon”. When npm install ran as root, the agent ran as root. From then on the attacker could give the server orders from a Telegram chat. The npm account zmaticoo published nine versions on 16 November 2026. SafeDep flagged the package five minutes after the last release, and npm has since removed it. In September, ThreatDown reported a botnet ⁠ (opens in new tab) that spreads through exposed Docker APIs and runs Hermes Agent as an implant. This is the first case SafeDep has seen of an npm install doing the same, with the agent’s persona downloaded at install time. The publisher is still active. Three packages it released on 18 November contain no code of their own and pull a dependency from the attacker’s server instead. The npm user zmaticoo (venstate25@gmail[.]com) published all nine versions between 09:44 and 15:27 UTC. The package described itself as “Official LeadStack CRM client”. Its early READMEs asked for “LeadStack partner access on npm (private org)”, and every version except the last set "access": "restricted" in publishConfig . HD Moore, Chief Research Officer, will be regularly sharing work from the research team he leads at Dragos. Topics will include xOT, IT, LLMs, PQC, and more. Their findings will sharpen defenders’ understanding of exposures and vulnerabilities emerging across the threat landscape. We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced. What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data. Over a five-month period from July through November 2026, we submitted approximately two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary token credentials to widely used AI services and monitored what happened after inference. Our investigation uncovered three significant findings: We wanted to understand what happens to inference data after it leaves the customer’s environment. To answer that question, we created millions of unique canaries, including URLs and credentials that would never be used by legitimate systems. Any attempt to access those assets would indicate that someone, somewhere in the AI ecosystem had seen the original prompt. The results exposed a fundamental disconnect between how AI services are marketed and how inference data is handled in practice. Most folks picture AI inference as a question and a response. Text goes in, GPUs juggle some bits, and text comes back out. What complicates this is how the data is actually treated. AI providers commonly store prompts and responses for operational, training, safety, abuse-monitoring, or business purposes. story|title:we let our ai save memories.content_excerpt: Small-business owners never opened the page where our AI's memory suggestions waited for approval, so it remembered almost nothing. We let it save on its own, then watched it remember a one-off request as a rule, a test question as a business plan and its own option list as a fact about the owner. The plain rules that fixed each one, and why every save now shows up under the answer with an Undo button. NEXUPIRA gives small-business owners a few AI coworkers: one drafts replies to customers and writes quotes, one keeps the books, one keeps the calendar. Like most assistants, they are much more useful when they remember things: what the shop sells, what it charges, when it opens, how the owner likes replies written. This post is about how we made that memory save itself, what went wrong in the two days of testing on our production site before we opened it to everyone, and the rules we added for each failure. Most of the rules are regular expressions and a word-overlap count. That is the point of the post. Our first design was careful. After a conversation, a background reader picked out facts worth remembering, and each one waited on a Memory page until the owner pressed Keep or Drop. Nothing reached the AI's memory without consent. It did not work, and not for a technical reason. Our users run nail salons, repair shops and one-person studios. They open the chat, ask for a quote, and leave. A queue on a settings page is invisible to them, so the AI kept asking for the same price list it had been told last week. A careful design that nobody uses protects no one; it only makes the product forget. So we changed the question. Instead of "should the owner approve every memory?" we asked: which facts are safe to save without asking, and how does the owner see and undo a save without going anywhere? The rules in step 3 work on the text alone, so they hold whatever the model says: The order matters. The things that must never be kept (passwords and API keys, bank and card numbers, customers' phone numbers, emails, chat-app IDs and addresses, a named person, health and family) are checked first and dropped, in English, Chinese and Japanese. Secrets are dropped even with the feature switched off: a key pasted into a chat must not even become a suggestion. A model can be talked into many things; a regular expression for sk-… or 「密碼」 cannot. Everything else that follows came from testing on production with real accounts.
